explore.welcome: Ohio has a lake breeze, rivers threading through the trees, and museums that can turn a quick stop into an afternoon. Its landscapes and communities each have a story to share. Pick the place that catches your eye, and we’ll follow its story. Bring your comfy shoes; there’s plenty to see. ♡

journeys.title: Three ways to meet the lake
journeys.intro: Ohio’s North Coast offers three ways to look closely. Toledo’s glass catches and bends the light; Magee Marsh rewards a patient eye for the smallest movement in a tree; offshore, the islands open onto a wide horizon. Each place has its own pace, and Lake Erie will be here whenever you return. ♡

stops.note: Toledo’s glass pavilion turns light into part of the artwork, with reflections that shift as visitors move around it. From here, Magee Marsh offers a quieter kind of close looking.
At Magee Marsh, one flicker in the leaves might be the whole event. Keep voices low and let the birds set the pace before heading toward open water. Shh…
The horizon opens across Lake Erie’s islands. Check ferry details before choosing an island, then leave time to enjoy its distinct shoreline and communities. Ooh, what a view.

journeys.title: The land holds more than one story
journeys.intro: Southern Ohio holds places shaped by different communities and histories. Glen Helen’s protected woodland rewards a slow walk; Serpent Mound is an Indigenous cultural place that calls for respect and careful attention; Hocking Hills reveals sandstone and water on a dramatic scale. Give each place its own visit, and let what you learn at one sharpen your attention at the next.

stops.note: Glen Helen’s woodland trails and Yellow Spring invite a slow walk through a small landscape rich in detail. That same patience serves visitors well at Serpent Mound.
Serpent Mound is an Indigenous cultural place. Read the site’s history, respect its boundaries, and pause before drawing conclusions. Carry that care onward when the route turns toward Hocking Hills.
Sandstone, steps, and stream-cut spaces give Hocking Hills a distinct feel. Choose a trail that suits the day and leave room to notice more than the waterfall.

homeSpotlight.text: Magee Marsh brings the North Coast to life with wings. Its boardwalk crosses wooded wetland beside Lake Erie, where spring migration draws warblers and other songbirds. The rest of the year has quieter discoveries, too. Bring binoculars if you have them; I’ll help you look for the next flutter. ♡

live.welcome: Ohio’s public life takes shape in its Statehouse, museums, trails, and neighborhood gardens. The people who care for these places, ask questions, and make decisions give them their meaning. Pick a door that makes you curious, and see what’s happening inside. ♡

journeys.title: A little closer to public life
journeys.intro: Three places hold different parts of Ohio’s public story: the Statehouse, where laws are discussed; the public record, where a bill’s progress can be followed; and a museum preserving lives and voices often left out of a quick civics lesson. These are separate visits and reading sessions across the state. Bring your questions; each stop may raise another worth following.

stops.note: Begin in the Statehouse Map Room, then follow a question about Ohio’s government into the public record. The building’s tours offer a close look at where public decisions take shape.
A proposal’s path from committee to vote makes the legislative process easier to follow. Choose a subject that matters to you and trace it through the official record.

At the National Afro-American Museum & Cultural Center in Wilberforce, an object or exhibition can bring individual lives into focus. Give those stories room and listen for whose experiences they preserve.

journeys.title: Follow your curiosity outside
journeys.intro: Ohio’s outdoor life grows through observation and care. Nature centers help visitors carry questions onto the trail; community gardens show what a season of tending can accomplish; local gatherings bring neighbors together. These stops span different cities and kinds of commitment, so choose one that fits the day and save the others for another chapter.

stops.note: Outside the Rocky River Nature Center, a small observation—a bird call, a leaf, a change in the path—can become a question to carry along the trail.
Possum Creek’s garden plots reward returning over time. Learn how the plots and volunteer opportunities work, then see what kind of commitment fits.
Local calendars show what neighbors are making together. Check what’s happening nearby, listen first, and offer a hand when it’s welcome. You might find a lovely surprise.

homeSpotlight.text: The National Afro-American Museum & Cultural Center in Wilberforce preserves stories through photographs, everyday objects, and writing. Each can open a life you haven’t met yet. Take your time with the story that stays with you.

make.welcome: Ohio’s work happens on wonderfully different scales. A ship unloads beside Lake Erie, a potter shapes a vessel, and a Columbus factory turns brass into a familiar sound. Across the state, people carry old skills forward and test what comes next. Follow the materials, routes, hands, and machines behind the things that reach everyday life. Ooh, there’s more to each story than meets the eye. ♡

journeys.title: Follow the freight
journeys.intro: Ohio’s freight story begins at working places like Toledo’s waterfront, then stretches across trade routes and the people and systems that keep deliveries moving. Follow a shipment through the chain and notice how many hands it passes through. The next box or piece of steel may carry a much longer story than it first appears to. Neat, right?

stops.note: Toledo’s waterfront makes freight movement visible: vessel, dock, crane, rail. Cargo arriving at a waterfront plant can become an ingredient for making something new.
The port is one connection among Ohio’s waterways, rail corridors, airports, and roads. Each route has a distinct role in moving materials and products between places.
Freight reaches its destination through the planning and work of people coordinating storage, transfers, timing, and the last stretch of delivery.

journeys.title: What a material becomes
journeys.intro: A tire, a ceramic tile, and a brass whistle show three different kinds of making. Their makers solve different problems, but each object begins with material that must be shaped, tested, and finished. Follow the work from Akron to Cincinnati to Columbus, and look beyond the finished surface to the decisions that made each object useful, beautiful, or unmistakable to the ear.

stops.note: A tire’s everyday familiarity hides years of design questions. Akron’s rubber story moves from early products to experiments that change how a wheel meets the road.
Clay asks for a different pace. Rookwood’s potters and tile makers give form and finish to objects meant for rooms, tables, and walls.
A small piece of brass becomes a dependable signal. The inspection step matters: someone checks whether the finished whistle actually sounds right.

homeSpotlight.text: A small brass whistle and a Great Lakes freighter both reveal the work behind everyday objects. Columbus makers shape brass into a signal you know by ear; across Ohio, materials, makers, and routes connect many more stories. There’s always another connection to find. ♡

culture.welcome: Ohio’s cultural life fills markets, galleries, stages, and everyday conversations. Shoppers and vendors keep a market moving; a library preserves comics as art and history; a museum gives rescued street signs a new home. Look for the people and memories behind each place. Take your time—I’ll be right here when you’re ready for another story. ♡

journeys.title: Rooms full of people
journeys.intro: A market, a sign museum, and a concert hall each show how people meet a place. Shoppers and vendors animate the market; signs recall the storefronts that once called to passersby; performers and audiences give a concert hall its sound. Ask what draws people through a door—and what brings them back.

stops.note: At West Side Market, notice the present tense: who is selling, choosing, and talking today? The historic building matters, and so do the people at its working counters.
The American Sign Museum shows how makers invited people into shops and streets through light, color, and lettering. Every rescued sign carries traces of the place where it once stood.
Cincinnati Music Hall comes alive through musicians, dancers, crews, and an audience. Together they make each performance an evening that happens only once.

journeys.title: Lines, images, and sound
journeys.intro: Art helps a place remember itself. Drawings once appeared on newspaper pages; museums care for works people want to keep; concert halls bring performances to a crowd. Follow this creative trail at your own pace and linger with the cartoon or song that speaks to you. Which work will stay with you afterward?

stops.note: A cartoon can be funny, angry, tender, or all three. The Billy Ireland Cartoon Library & Museum preserves original work and the context behind what readers once saw in print.
Ohio’s galleries and museums hold many forms of creative work. Choose a collection or exhibition that makes you look twice, then give it enough time.
At Severance, the Cleveland Orchestra builds one sound from many instruments. Notice the room, then let the music give it a voice.

homeSpotlight.text: Cleveland’s West Side Market has welcomed shoppers since 1912. The people behind its counters keep the busy room alive today. From vendors to artists, archivists, and performers, Ohio’s cultural voices are made by the people who share their work. ♡
